Sweep Backtest (SBT)

6300 optimizer configurations over one FIXED curation (data/cbt_3yr_v8) · no LLM, no re-curation · knobs from investor_profile.backtest.md

1. Parameter settings

The 6 FREE swept knobs — every combination is a cell, 4×3×7×3×5×5 = 6300 configs — and the values considered. These knobs only RE-WEIGHT a fixed set of curator picks, which is what makes the grid free: no LLM call is made and no event is discovered or closed differently. max_events is the exception and is listed last: it is a CURATION knob, deciding which events stay live and therefore which tickers ever reach the optimizer, so each of its values needed a full re-curation rather than a replay — see the cost column, and panels 10–13. Every other optimizer / curator parameter is held at its investor_profile.backtest.md value.

2. Return vs drawdown

The horizontal axis is max drawdown — the book's biggest peak-to-trough loss as a fraction of its running peak; further right = deeper loss. The vertical axis is annualized return, so upper-left is best. Each point is one config; colour is the share of the winners' gains handed back by the losers, so a pale point in the upper-left is the whole objective at once. The live config is the purple ★ star.

3. Return vs L1 churn

Same points, risk axis replaced by L1 churn = annualized one-way turnover (Σ|Δweight| across rebalances, ×100/yr): how much of the book is traded per year. Weights are held flat between rebalances, so drift never counts as a trade. Trading is free in an IRA, so read this as stability, not cost: lower churn = less noise-chasing and less overfit, making upper-left the sweet spot. Colour is Sharpe: a dark point at high churn is trading that actually pays for itself.

4. Return vs L2 course correction

Same idea, but the path length the book was dragged through weight-space (√ΣΔweight² per rebalance, summed and annualized). Against L1 it weights concentrated single-name rotations more heavily. The useful read is whether the two norms rank configs alike — if they do, the churn ordering is robust rather than an artefact of which norm was picked. Coloured by Sharpe, as panel 3.

5. Return vs Sharpe

The same cloud with Sharpe on the horizontal — return per unit of volatility, the measure table 6 actually ranks by. This is the one panel here where upper-RIGHT is best, since higher Sharpe is better; every other risk axis on this page reads the other way. Colour is max drawdown, pinned to the same 20–120% band as panel 6 so the two are comparable. The cloud is a tight rising diagonal — return and Sharpe correlate +0.92 across the grid, so for most configs they say the same thing and there is no return/risk trade to agonise over. The divergence is all in the tail, which is exactly where a config gets picked. On this book the grid's biggest final value ($1.52M, 225%/yr) ranks only 1,351st of 6,300 by Sharpe — 79th percentile — because it earns that return on a 59% drawdown. The best-Sharpe cell (1.93) makes $401K on a 24% drawdown instead. Read the top-right corner, not the top edge: a point that is high but far left is return bought with volatility a live account has to actually sit through.

6. Return vs cancellation

The fourth view of the same points, and the one that matters most: the horizontal axis is the share of the winners' gains handed back by the losers, so upper-left is best — a book that earns and keeps it. Colour is max drawdown, so a pale upper-left point earns well, keeps it, and does so without a deep hole. The cloud's shape is itself the finding: if it were a tight rising diagonal these knobs would only be trading return against cancellation, and it is not one.

7. Return vs second-half slope

Return against when it arrived. The horizontal is the second-half slope — (final − midpoint) ÷ 1.5 years, in dollars per year — so a point far right was still compounding in the back half of the run, and a point at or left of zero made its money early and then coasted or gave it back. Upper-right is best. Colour is max drawdown, on the same 20–120% band as panels 5 and 6.

The cloud is a tight rising diagonal — return and slope correlate +0.95, tighter even than return and Sharpe — so for almost every config the two say the same thing. That tightness is the finding, and it is a warning about slope, not a recommendation of it: a measure this correlated with return carries almost no information return does not, which is consistent with slope ranking configs at the 53rd percentile on the re-curation transfer test, i.e. no better than random. Only 4 of 6,300 cells clear 50%/yr while finishing with a negative slope, so the made-it-early-then-coasted failure this panel was built to expose barely happens on this book. 863 cells (14%) do have a negative slope, but they are the low-return cells you would drop anyway.

Two things to read carefully. The 95 cells above $500K/yr are clipped at the right edge rather than allowed to flatten the rest (the maximum is $2.0M/yr). And the two axes are computed off different equity curves — annualized return compounds rebalance-window to rebalance-window while slope comes from the daily series, which for the live config end at $302,079 and $460,556 respectively. The rank ordering is unaffected, but do not read a ratio off this panel. Blue squares are table 9's top 100 — all 100 have a positive slope, median $151,140/yr.

8. Gains on the no-brainer shortlist

What each config made on seven names that were obvious in hindsight — big multi-year rises where the press named dated catalysts, not narrative: RKLB, DRUG, MU, BE, IREN, MP, QUBT, one per sector so nothing wins by loading a single theme. Vertical is dollars on those seven, horizontal is Sharpe, colour is cancellation — upper-right and pale earns well, keeps it, and gets paid for the obvious ones; below the zero line it lost money on names that rose 120–3,590%. No robotics: our corpus carries 1 article on RCAT (+868%), 0 on UMAC (+762%) and 3 on ONDS (+699%) but 90 on PATH (−1%), so that sector is a hole in our news feed, not a config failure. Blue squares are table 9's top five (rank on hover); the purple ★ is the live config.

9. Recommended settings

The shortlist: every config clearing all five gates — max DD < 65% · L1 > 2000%/yr · L2 750–1350/yr · Sharpe > 0.8 · cancelled < 65% — 2288 of 6,300 survive. Ranked by robust — the mean of a config's cancellation rank and its drawdown rank across the whole sweep, 0 = best. This ordering was chosen by measurement, not argument: the only clean test available is the noise-experiment pair (me16 and rep, the same settings curated twice, differing only in LLM sampling). Ranking all 6,300 configs on one and scoring that top 50 on the other puts cancellation+drawdown at the 86th percentile of the re-curation, plateau at the 83rd, Sharpe at the 54th — a coin flip — and final value at the 43rd, worse than random. Ranking a shortlist by P&L selects one curation's luck. The plateau and #Sharpe columns are kept beside it: where they disagree with the order is exactly where the overfit risk lives.neighbours'), not Sharpe: every row here already passed the bars, so the question is not which is best in sample but which still works on the NEXT curation — and Sharpe-ranking put a cell at row 1 whose own 1.93 falls to 1.29 one step away, in a project that has had three sweep winners fail to survive a re-curation. The #Sharpe column keeps both views, because where the two disagree is where the overfit risk is. Note the live config [8, 0.25, 14, 0, 4.0, 0.20] misses by 0.0 — cancellation 20.0 against a < 20% bar; a ★ marks the best survivor per column, top 100 shown, current config on the last row.

10. drop_unfunded_weeks × lookback_period_days

Median cancellation at each combination of the two knobs whose marginals span the widest range. This is the panel a 1-D sweep cannot produce, and it is where the interactions hide — a value that looks harmless on average can be the worst choice in one corner of the grid.

11. Each knob on its own

For every value of every knob: the MEDIAN cancellation across all cells holding that value (the bar) and the BEST single cell (the dot). A wide gap between them means the knob only pays in combination with something else. The live setting is outlined.

12. Portfolio value vs max_events

The one knob on this page that is not free to sweep. Everything above replays a FIXED curation through different book math, so 6,300 cells cost nothing; max_events decides which events stay live and so which tickers ever reach the optimizer, meaning each point here is a full re-curation ($22.89 and several hours for the series). Bars are final portfolio value and, beside it, the gain on the six no-brainer names from panel 8 — same axis, same unit. The line is the share of events culled at birth — opened and retired without a single agent read, i.e. work paid for and thrown away. Read the CULL LINE first: it is a structural count the cap moves directly, while final value is one lucky name away from noise, and each point is a single stochastic sample (the scout is an LLM; two runs at the same cap would differ). A monotone trend across the six is worth something; a one-point spike in dollars is not.

13. Risk-adjusted quality vs max_events

Sharpe per cap, against the > 0.8 floor the current gate set uses. Read it beside panel 12: a cap that wins on final value while dropping below the floor has not won anything the shortlist would admit. Sharpe is NOT what table 9 ranks by — that is robust, cancellation rank + drawdown rank — and Sharpe measured at the 54th percentile on the re-curation transfer test, i.e. a coin flip. It is kept here as a gate and a sanity column, not as a ranking.

14. Where the money sits, and what it gives back

Three percentages on ONE axis, all of them defects: max drawdown (the hole the book digs), cancellation (winners' gains handed back by losers) and idle days (days holding NO position at all — the cash band in CBT plot 9). Dashed lines are the shortlist bars, DD < 35% and cancellation < 25%. Idle days is the one that ties this knob to the optimizer: a tight cap starves the watchlist, so the book sits in cash not because the curator ran out of theses but because it was never allowed to open them. All three are better LOW, so a cap whose three bars are all short is the one to want.

15. What the cap costs, and what it buys

Left bars: the LLM bill for that curation — the only thing on this page that is not free, since each point is a full re-curation rather than a replay. Right bars: the same money divided by tickers that actually got funded, which is the efficiency question — a cap that opens hundreds of events the optimizer never funds is paying the event-agent bill for reading it may as well not have done. Only the agent half of the bill scales with the cap; the scout reads the same ticker-groups either way, which is why the left bars flatten while the cap keeps rising.

16. Portfolio value vs LLM spend

Portfolio value after event_agent_model is swept — the LLM that judges, every scan, whether each thesis is still live. Eight runs spanning 5.3× in price ($5.96 to $31.66), each a whole 3-year curation re-run. Everything else is identical: same scout, same 99,117-article corpus, same optimizer settings. Final value barely tracks price, and seven of the eight bars land inside the shaded band — the noise floor I measured beforehand by curating the same settings twice, which came out 1.86× apart. The one exception is Grok 4.3 at low reasoning, the second-cheapest arm. So a pricier judgment model buys no return I can measure here, and that band is what lets me say so rather than guess. The gold line is wall-clock: price and speed are unrelated — the cheapest arm was also the slowest, by 4×.

17. What the money actually buys: decision quality vs spend

Grey bars are what a cheap model made of all 4,527 event-agent decisions; green bars are that verdict after Claude Fable-5 re-read samples of both what it flagged and what it passed. I scored process only — was the catalyst datable, did the write-up outrun the evidence it cited, did the live/exit call contradict its own stated exit condition — with no prices in front of the judge. Quality separates here where portfolio value in panel 16 did not, and it peaks in the middle: GPT-5.6 Luna at $13 leads on 63.8%, Grok 4.3 at $6 is within three points, and Claude Sonnet 5 — the priciest arm at $32 — finishes LAST.

18. Where each model actually fails

Panel 17's three tests, split out. dated asks whether the catalyst is a specific resolvable event — a contract award, a ruling, an FDA decision — rather than an open-ended trend like “AI demand grows”; every model is weakest here (46–66%), and since that holds across eight runs and six vendors it is my prompt at fault, not them. supported asks whether the write-up follows from the evidence it actually cited or claims more certainty than those sources carry — the only axis that really separates models, GPT-5.6 Luna at 97% against DeepSeek's 75%. consistent asks whether the live/exit call contradicts the analyst's own stated exit condition; nobody does, so at 94–100% it separates nothing and can be retired.

19. The bake-off, in full

Every arm, every measure, ordered by LLM spend. Cancellation, drawdown and Sharpe are book behaviour; dated / supported / clean are decision quality; final value is the number that cannot be trusted alone. Read the last three columns against the first: the correlation between what an arm costs and what its book returns is the thing this table exists to let you check for yourself.

20. Is the judge any good?

The obvious objection to panels 17–19 is that an LLM graded the LLMs, so here is the grader's own audit. Left bars: how often the cheap screen and Fable-5 reached the same verdict, per process test. They agree 95% of the time on consistent (did the call contradict its own stated exit condition? — nearly mechanical), 84% on dated, and only 65% on supported — deciding whether a write-up asserts more than its citations carry is exactly the judgment a cheap model gets wrong, which is the thesis of this whole exercise showing up inside its own measurement.

Right bars are the load-bearing number: how much of each arm's flagged pile Fable-5 threw out. The tier-1 ranking only survives correction because those rates are SIMILAR across arms (24–33%). Had one arm been overturned at 60% and another at 10%, the ordering in panel 17 would be an artefact of the cheap screen's biases rather than a real difference between models.

Gold bars are why the audit had to be two-sided. Re-reading only what the screen FLAGGED corrects false accusations and is blind to false clearances, so every rate would have been an upper bound. Fable-5 also read 250 decisions the screen PASSED and condemned 15% of them — but that rate runs 8% to 28% by arm, and correcting it moved the cheapest model from 4th place to LAST. A one-sided audit would have published the wrong ranking. Caveat, stated not buried: 500 of 1,673 flags and 250 of 1,164 passes were re-read, stratified per arm — enough to estimate these rates, but samples. Reading every flagged decision alone would have cost $59 against $25 budgeted.
